'''''Pandanus odorifer''''' is an aromatic monocot species of [[plant]] in the family [[Pandanaceae]], native to South East Asia, the [[Andaman Islands]], the [[Philippines]], and is also found wild in southern [[India]] and [[Burma]].<ref>{{citation |author1=Nadaf, A. |title=Indian Pandanaceae - an overview |pages=15–28 |year=2012 |chapter=Biogeography of Indian Pandanaceae |publisher=Springer India |doi=10.1007/978-81-322-0753-5_3 |isbn=978-81-322-0752-8 |author2=Zanan, R.}}</ref> It is commonly known as '''fragrant screw-pine'''.

==Names==
In addition to screw-pine, other common English names for the tree include ''kewda'', ''fragrant screwpine'', ''umbrella tree'' and ''screw tree''.<ref name="FOI">[https://www.flowersofindia.net/catalog/slides/Kewda.html "Kewda".] FlowersOfIndia.net. Retrieved 25 July 2016.</ref>

In India, the tree goes by a variety of names, many deriving from the Sanskrit ''kētakī''.<ref name="FOI"/> in [[Kannada]] called '' ಕೇದಿಗೆ'' <ref name="FOI"/>  in [[Malayalam]] called ''pookkaitha'' and its flower known as ''thaazhampoo'', In [[Tamil language|Tamil]], it is called ''kaithai'' ([[:ta:கைதை|கைதை]]) and ''tāḻai'' ([[:ta:தாழை|தாழை]]) and both are mentioned in [[Sangam literature]]. It is called ''mogali'' ([[:te:మొగలి|మొగలి]]) in [[Telugu language|Telugu]]. In Arabic-speaking countries, the tree is referred to as ''al-kādī'' ({{langx|ar|الكادي}}).<ref name="J.R.I. Wood, 1997, p. 315">J.R.I. Wood, ''A Handbook of the Yemen Flora'', Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew 1997, p. 315 {{ISBN|1 900347 31 8}}</ref>  In Japan, the tree is called ''adan'' ({{lang|ja|アダン [阿檀]}}) and grows throughout most of the islands of [[Okinawa Prefecture]], including the [[Okinawa Islands]] and [[Sakishima Islands]], as well as the [[Tokara Islands]] and [[Amami Islands]] of [[Kagoshima Prefecture]].

''P. odorifer'' grows widely at the [[St. Martin's Island]] of [[Bangladesh]], although many have been destroyed by mass tourism initiatives.

==Description==
It is a small branched, palm-like [[dioecy|dioecious]] tree with a flexuous trunk supported by [[brace roots]]. The tree can grow to a height of 4 meters. Leaves grow in clusters at the branch tips, with rosettes of sword-shaped, stiff  (leather-like) and spiny bluish-green, fragrant leaves. Leaves are glaucous, 40–70 cm. long. In summer, the tree bears very fragrant flowers, used as perfume. Interestingly, Pandanus lacks a common [[callose]] wall around [[microspore]] tetrads during [[pollen]] development.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Scott |first=R. J. |date=2004-03-12 |title=Stamen Structure and Function |journal=The Plant Cell Online |language=en |volume=16 |issue=suppl_1 |pages=S46–S60 |doi=10.1105/tpc.017012 |issn=1040-4651 |pmc=2643399 |pmid=15131249}}</ref> In [[Yemen]], they are predominantly found alongside flowing streams in the western escarpment foothills; Most common in high rainfall areas.<ref>Abdul Wali A. al-Khulaidi, ''Flora of Yemen'', Sustainable Environmental Management Program (YEM/97/100), Republic of Yemen, June 2000, pp. 13, 149.</ref> The fragrant male flowers are wrapped in leaves and sold on roadsides and in markets. Only male plants seem to occur in Yemen.<ref name="J.R.I. Wood, 1997, p. 315"/> Some suggest that it was introduced into Yemen from India where its flowers are used chiefly to make perfume.

==Propagation==
The tree is propagated vegetatively, by the offshoots of young plants that grow around the base of the trunk, but may also be increased by seed. If by the former method, the offshoots should be cut off and set in sand, at a temperature of 65° to 70 °F. The cuttings root slowly, and the plants for a time grow very slowly. The general treatment required for culturing the screw-pine is similar to that of palms. Trees require an abundance of water in summer.<ref>[http://www.gutenberg.org/files/9550/9550-h/files/chVIII.htm L.H. Bailey, Manual of Gardening (2nd edition), New York 1910, Chapter VIII: The Growing of the Ornamental Plants – Instructions of Particular Kinds], s.v. Pandanus.</ref>

According to [[Ibn al-'Awwam]]'s 12th-century treatise on agriculture, the ''kadi'' is cultivated in a manner similar to that of the Judas tree (''[[Cercis siliquastrum]]'').<ref>{{cite book|last=Ibn al-'Awwam|first=Yaḥyá|author-link=Ibn al-'Awwam|title=Le livre de l'agriculture d'Ibn-al-Awam (kitab-al-felahah) |year=1864|location=Paris|publisher=A. Franck|translator=J.-J. Clement-Mullet |page=304 (ch. 7 - Article 35)|url=https://archive.org/details/lelivredelagric00algoog/page/n14/mode/2up |language=fr|oclc=780050566}} (p. [https://archive.org/details/lelivredelagric00algoog/page/n412/mode/2up 304], Article XXXV). For the cultivating method of the Judas tree, see pp. [https://archive.org/details/lelivredelagric00algoog/page/n410/mode/2up 303]–304.</ref>

==Other uses==
An aromatic oil called [[kewra]] and a fragrant distillate called ''keorra-ka-arak'' are extracted from the male flowers.<ref name="Adkar2014">{{cite journal |vauthors=Adkar PP, Bhaskar VH |date=22 December 2014 |title=''Pandanus odoratissimus'' (Kewda): A Review on Ethnopharmacology, Phytochemistry, and Nutritional Aspects |journal=Adv. Pharmacol. Sci. |volume=2014 |article-number=120895 |doi=10.1155/2014/120895 |pmc=4408760 |pmid=25949238 |doi-access=free |number=120895}}</ref> They are almost exclusively used in the form of a watery distillate called kewra water. Its flowers have a sweet, perfumed odor that has a pleasant quality similar to rose flowers, although ''kewra'' is considered more fruity. The watered-down distillate is quite diluted; it can be used by the tablespoon.

The ketaki tree's flower is never used as an offering to the god [[Shiva]]. According to Hindu mythology, Shiva cursed the flower that it will never be used to worship him for helping Brahma lie against him, and then to Brahma that he will not be worshipped by people.

On [[Ishigaki Island]], south-west of Okinawa, it is customary to use parts of the plant during [[Bon (festival)|Bon]] festivities as an offering. The soft shoots can also be eaten, although the taste is very astringent and the shoots are considered inedible without [[Blanching (cooking)|blanching]] them first. When they are properly treated however, the taste is similar to that of bamboo shoots.

Despite the pineapple-like appearance of the fruit and its sweet aroma, it is very fibrous and while being non-toxic, is generally not considered for consumption.
